Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for Australia's response with the bat! The umpires and players are out to the middle. Sri Lankan players spread out to their respective fielding positions. Out walks the Australian opening pair of Matthew Short and Jake Fraser-McGurk. Asitha Fernando has the new ball and will kickoff the Sri Lankan defence with a couple of slips in place. Short to face and off we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Well then, we have seen some remarkable resistance from Sri Lanka's skipper when the rest of the batters faltered. But now, it is time for the bowlers to step up and perform. Since it is a day game, the pitch will slow down further and that's where the Sri Lankan spinners could come handy. But if Sri Lanka are to win this game, they will have to snag all ten wickets of this potent Australian batting unit that bats deep. Stick around, as the run chase is up next shortly.

Nathan Ellis is up for a quick chat and says that he is feeling good and went in not knowing what the wicket would be like. Adds that it is a good performance nonetheless. Says that a lot of boys came in from the Big Bash League into these hot conditions, so adapting was key. Mentions that at the start if you said 214 on the board, they would have taken it with both hands. Adds that the ball nipped around in the first 10 overs. Hopefully, the boys will go out there and do the job. When asked about spin, he said that it is not sure how much of a role spin will play and concludes by saying that Short and Adam Zampa bowled well.

Asalanka, proved to be a crisis man for Sri Lanka. He first faced the dual responsibility of scoring runs and guiding the tailenders. With partners falling around him, Asalanka stood firm, ensuring his side surpassed a significant milestone and also reached a century of his own. Eshan Malinga's modest contribution proved a valuable foil to his captain. In order to avoid the risk of being bowled out before the allotted overs, Asalanka protected the tail and consistently found boundaries once he had settled in. But once he fell, Australia went for the kill, but not before Sri Lanka crossed over the 200-run mark.

Amidst a challenging situation, Charith Asalanka's experience shone through as he strategically found boundaries while keeping the score moving. Dunith Wellalage offered valuable support, skillfully maneuvering the ball to sustain their partnership. Just as Asalanka and Wellalage found their rhythm, adeptly handling the spinners through the middle overs, the innings faced further setbacks. Wickets fell consistently at the other end, but Asalanka remained steadfast.

Sri Lanka's technical frailties proved contagious, with static feet leading to a procession of edges - batters repeatedly fishing outside off with their feet stuck in crease. It was a dream day for Australia's makeshift pace attack. Despite missing their frontline pacers to injury, the understudies stepped up brilliantly. Abbott and Ellis, though relatively experienced, also looked right at home with accurate lines and lengths.

After the early carnage, Asalanka and Liyanage shouldered the rescue mission, but runs came at a crawl against Australia's stranglehold. Steven Smith kept the pressure cooker on with tight fields, forcing the Lankan pair to scrap for every run. Just when their partnership threatened to shift momentum, Sean Abbott shattered the resistance, leaving Sri Lanka back at square one.

On a bone-dry surface that promised little, Australia's pacers crafted a masterclass in new ball bowling. Spencer Johnson and Aaron Hardie exploited whatever movement was on offer, while Sri Lanka's batters struggled with their footwork. By the time the dust settled, the scoreboard read a worrying 39/4 inside the first Powerplay. The decimation of the top order, including key men Nissanka and Kusal Mendis, left Sri Lanka staring down the barrel early in the piece.

From losing half of their side on a meager score of 55, Sri Lanka have ended their innings with a total of 214 on the board. Yes, they will be disappointed that they couldn't bat for the allotted overs, but this innings potentially could've been wrapped up way before had Charith Asalanka not stepped up and mounted a strong resistance with the bat. Also, as per the on-air commentators, Sri Lanka might feel they left 15-20 runs than the par score here and could have gone past that had they played the remaining overs.

Opts to defend it down with a straight bat but the ball moves away just enough to catch the outside edge. The keeper Alex Carey snaffles it to his right. Sri Lanka have been bowled out for 214!

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS BREAK! Nathan Ellis gets in on the act for Australia, and this wicket has now opened one end for the tourists. With Australia into the tail, the pressure is mounting on Charith Asalanka, who will need to shepherd the tail and farm the strike to help Sri Lanka post a competitive total. Even during this middle phase, the movement off the deck has been evident, and the Aussie seamers have exploited it to great effect. They will be keen to wrap things up quickly, relying on their pacers to finish off the tail and bowl Sri Lanka out for a modest total. Maheesh Theekshana is the new man in.

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS BREAK. Australian bowlers have run through half of the Sri Lankan batting line up and all it has taken them to do so is just under 15 overs. Just when it seemed that this partnership for the fifth wicket was blossoming into something meaningful, Sean Abbott broke that resistance. But before, Spencer Johnson and Aaron Hardie set the tone for the tourists by keeping the batters under immense pressure with tight lines and movement off the deck. Lack of footwork has been Sri Lanka's nemesis so far as more than half of the wickets fallen are off the edges and no footwork. Sri Lanka desperately needs a partnership here as there's a lot of overs to spare. Skipper Asalanka will need a steady partner at the other end to bail the hosts out of the turbulent waters. Here's Dunith Wellalage in at number 7.

OUT! EDGED AND GONE! Abbott breaks through and brings about an end to Janith's resistance. On a good length, in the corridor of off from over the wicket, Janith commits the same mistake as Sri Lanka's top three batters. His absence adds to Australia's growing concerns, with Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, and Mitchell Marsh already sidelined by injuries, and Marcus Stoinis announcing a shock retirement.

After a commanding Test series whitewash against Sri Lanka, Australia now shift gears for a crucial two-match ODI series, one that holds immense significance ahead of the Champions Trophy. With injury concerns and last-minute changes shaking up their squad, the Aussies find themselves in a race against time to assemble a formidable unit for the marquee tournament. Sri Lanka, despite missing out on Champions Trophy action, have stuck with a familiar squad, largely unchanged from their recent series against New Zealand. The action unfolds at the iconic R. Premadasa Stadium in Colombo, setting the stage for an intense battle. Following a dismal Test series, Sri Lanka have plenty to prove, particularly their ability to handle spin on home soil, a surprising Achilles’ heel. This ODI series presents the perfect chance to regain lost confidence and inject fresh momentum. Pathum Nissanka will be desperate to return to his best form, while the batting unit, bolstered by Kusal Mendis and Kamindu Mendis alongside skipper Charith Asalanka, looks solid. Meanwhile, the spin duo of Maheesh Theekshana and Wanindu Hasaranga will be key, with Asitha Fernando spearheading the pace attack. Sticking to a consistent squad signals Sri Lanka’s intent to build winning momentum, regardless of their tournament absence, a promising sign for their future. Australia, on the other hand, are in a whirlwind just days before the Champions Trophy. Skipper Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood’s absence has left Mitchell Starc as the lone pace veteran, forcing a major reshuffle. The big question remains. Will they risk playing Starc in this series or preserve him for the grand stage? To further complicate matters, Mitchell Marsh’s back injury and Marcus Stoinis’ shock retirement have rattled the middle order, leaving the team’s balance in disarray. In response, Sean Abbott, Spencer Johnson and Ben Dwarshuis have been drafted in, along with leg-spinner Tanveer Sangha and all-rounder Cooper Connolly. Jake Fraser-McGurk could also step up as Marsh’s replacement. With so many new faces and limited time to gel, Australia will be eager to give their fresh recruits valuable game time before the main event. Adding to the suspense, Australia are yet to announce their captain for both this series and the Champions Trophy. Steven Smith appears to be the frontrunner, but Travis Head remains a strong contender. Despite a depleted squad, Australia’s batting firepower is still intimidating, making them a tough challenge for Sri Lanka. The hosts, however, see this as a golden opportunity to capitalize on a vulnerable opponent and make a statement in a format they have thrived in recently. All signs point to an enthralling series!
